LEARNING PATH LESSON · VEHICLES & SOUNDS · AGES 2 YEARS

Excavator — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson surrenders to the inevitable: your toddler loves diggers. Scoop, swing, dump, repeat — with both words on offer, digger for now and excavator for delight.

What is this?

An excavator is a digging machine with a long arm and a bucket that goes dig dig — called a digger by everyone under four.

What does it mean?

Two names for one machine is a first synonym: digger and excavator. Say both without pressure — the long word is a treat, the short one is the working vocabulary.

What does the child need to know?

The arm scoops, swings and dumps — three verbs in one machine. Pair the card with any digging toy and the afternoon arranges itself; a bowl of dry cereal upgrades it further.

Why this matters

This is the card a two-year-old requests at breakfast, lunch and dinner. Favoured cards do the teaching on their own; your job is to keep the scoop moving.

What it teaches

Action verbs (dig, scoop, swing, dump), fine-motor scooping practice, and the pride of owning a long word most grown-ups fumble.

Words to learn

excavatordiggerdigscoopbucketdump

Say this to your child

“"Digger! Or — excavator, if you are feeling fancy. Dig dig dig! Can you scoop? Swing the arm… and DUMP! Look at those wheels and that long arm. Again!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card and say digger, then excavator slowly, like a treat — and dig dig with your arm as the bucket.
  2. Scoop together: spoon-digger into a bowl of dry rice or cereal — scoop, swing, dump — narrating each verb as it happens.
  3. Hunt diggers in books and from windows; real excavators on building sites are visible from a long way off, which helps.
  4. When your toddler says brrm or digs without the sound, supply the dig dig and cheer the digging — verbs land one at a time.
  5. Keep the bowl and spoon set up this week; a standing digging station means the card teaches itself between meals.

Look closer at the picture

The label says Excavator and the words Dig dig sit under it. Follow the long arm with one finger — where does it end? In the bucket.

Ask your child

"Where is the excavator?" "What does the arm do?" "Can you scoop and dump?" "Which word is longer — digger or excavator?"

What your child can say or do

"Dig dig!" with a spoon, or the full excavator attempt which lands as ek-ka-vator and is entirely wonderful. The dump is always louder than the dig.

Out in the real world

Building sites, roadworks and sandpits are excavator country. Behind the hoarding, watch a real arm work one full cycle — scoop, swing, dump — and the card comes home pre-taught.

Try it together

Sandpit site: bucket as the truck bed, spoon as the excavator arm, and a load of sand or pasta moved one scoop at a time. Grown-up operates the site canteen; tea breaks are mandatory.

Understanding check

Ask what the excavator does with its arm. A dig, a scoop or a dump — any verb passes; all three is a full shift. Then listen for excavator arriving in pieces over the week.

Parent tips

Say both names often and let your toddler pick a favourite — the chewiness of a long word is a pleasure some toddlers refuse to give up. Freeze the digging bowl when it needs a break, not the game.

Staying safe

Real diggers work behind fences and hoardings for good reason — watch from outside the barrier, and keep the spoon-digger out of the dog’s bowl and the plug socket alike.

This lesson pairs with the Excavator flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Vehicles & Sounds (Toddler 6).
